ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Sensory physiology explains how receptors convert stimuli into nerve impulses, how the nervous system interprets these signals, and how the body adapts to persistent stimuli. Clinicians use this knowledge to diagnose sensory disorders and guide treatment.

sections.p: Sensory physiology studies how external and internal stimuli are detected by specialized receptors, transduced into electrical signals, and transmitted to the brain for interpretation.
b: Sensory receptors: mechanoreceptors, thermoreceptors, nociceptors, photoreceptors, chemoreceptors

sections.p: Stimulus activates a receptor, opening ion channels and generating a receptor potential. If threshold is reached, an action potential travels along afferent fibers to the spinal cord or brainstem, where it is processed.
b: Law of Specific Nerve Energies: each nerve fiber type carries a specific modality (e.g., Aδ for sharp pain).
Law of Projection: the brain interprets signals based on their origin, not the stimulus itself.

t.b: Assesses conduction velocity of sensory pathways; abnormal latency suggests demyelination.
Evaluates optic nerve function; delayed peaks indicate optic neuritis or demyelination.

sections.p: Sensory systems are modulated by central and peripheral mechanisms. Adaptation reduces response to sustained stimuli, while attention and expectation can amplify perception.
b: Rapid adaptation in mechanoreceptors reduces pain after initial shock.

sections.p: Damage or dysfunction of receptors, nerves, or central pathways leads to sensory loss, hyperesthesia, or dysesthesia. Common causes include infections, metabolic disorders, and trauma.

t.b: Measures conduction velocity and amplitude; low amplitude suggests axonal loss.

sections.p: Understanding sensory physiology helps clinicians interpret symptoms, choose appropriate tests, and tailor treatments for conditions such as neuropathic pain, visual field loss, and hearing impairment.
b: Pain management: use of anticonvulsants for neuropathic pain.

sections.p: Remember the three laws of sensory physiology, the concept of adaptation, and the typical patterns of sensory loss in common neuropathies.
b: Sharp pain travels via Aδ fibers; dull pain via C fibers.

sections.p: Treat underlying cause, provide symptomatic relief, and monitor for progression. Use drug classes that target specific pathways and avoid those with high toxicity in low‑resource settings.
b: Anticonvulsants (e.g., gabapentin) for neuropathic pain; avoid high‑dose opioids if liver function is compromised.

sections.p: Sensory loss can mimic motor deficits; differentiate by testing reflexes and strength.
Normal nerve conduction may miss early demyelination; low glucose may be falsely normal in hypoglycemia episodes.
b: False‑negative NCS in early diabetic neuropathy.

sections.p: Select tests based on suspected pathology and resource availability.

t.b: Assesses protective sensation in diabetic feet; loss predicts ulcer risk.
Detects optic nerve damage in diabetes or hypertension.

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained loss of sensation with weakness

faq.a: It is the decrease in response to a constant stimulus, allowing the nervous system to focus on new changes.

faq.q: How does the law of specific nerve energies help in diagnosis?
faq.a: It explains why different fibers carry distinct modalities, guiding targeted tests for specific sensory deficits.

faq.q: Why is the law of projection important clinically?
faq.a: It reminds clinicians that the brain interprets signals based on their origin, not the stimulus, influencing pain perception.

exam: Explain the three laws of sensory physiology and give an example of each.
Describe how peripheral neuropathy presents and outline the first‑line investigations.
